PA R T A · S TA R T H E R E

Welcome, Thinking Paleontologist

My name:                                 Date:
This is your Level 2 workbook (Development, ages 8–10). A paleontologist digs out evidence, reads the layers
and argues for what it means. You will do the same with ten stories this year.
Every story has four lessons. Every lesson has one page. The pages always go in the same order, and they
match the Level 2 Teacher Pack lesson by lesson:
    Excavation. Find exactly what the story says and what it suggests.
    Strata. Weigh two sides of a Big Question and take a position.
    Justification. Build the CEIW argument: Claim, Evidence, Interpretation, Warrant.
    Impact. Connect the story to the real world and the living world.

Your rule for evidence. Every quotation you write comes from the story, is short, and has a chapter
number. An opinion without evidence is not enough. The warrant, which explains why the evidence proves
your claim, is the most important move.
Word Fossils. Collect strong words as you read. Record them in the Fossil Log at the end of the book.

Story 1: The Bell That Rang Too Early

My name:                                     Date:
Lessons 1 to 4. Read the story in your printed Storybook Workbook, or have it read aloud to you. It has six
chapters.
A bell rings before the market is ready. Pavi thinks she knows who did it—but the clues point somewhere
else.
The big idea. What is someone worth when they are not useful yet, and how do we find out what really
happened before we blame?
Before I read: what do I predict?

    before checking)                              see a place)

Lesson 3 · The Justification: build the CEIW scaffold

My name:                               Date:
☐ Butterfly Hug ☐ Cool Down Pass ☐ Bilateral tapping (tick what you used before you started)
Claim to build on (from your Lesson 2 Claim Strip):

 Box                            What to write

 CLAIM                          My position, in one sentence.


 EVIDENCE                       An exact quotation from the story, with its chapter number.


 INTERPRETATION                 What the quotation means, in my own words.


 WARRANT                        Use the stem: This evidence supports my claim because                        .



MY FINISHED PARAGRAPH




Grown-up: quotations are copied from the story. Mark the claim, evidence, interpretation and warrant in
four colours.

Lesson 4 · Impact: Systemic causality and nature

My name:                                Date:
☐ Butterfly Hug ☐ Cool Down Pass ☐ Bilateral tapping (tick what you used before you started)
Reflect. Think of an animal or a plant that people value only for what it gives them (a hen for eggs, a tree for
wood). What happens to the land and to other living things when we count only what is useful?

 A human action or natural event        The first effect             The second effect                 What happens to nature

                                        →                            →



(one thing leads to the next)
Worked starter from the story: Rain falls on the market awning
MY REFLECTION: 2 TO 3 COMPLETE SENTENCES. Name a real place. For example, a rainwater bucket,
tank or pond near your own home or school.




Grown-up: the reflection must name a real system or place. Praise precise vocabulary and honest
uncertainty.
